body:
RAISED BY THE T174 BUILD LANE, in its own words, after that ticket's fence was breached three times by
independent review: "a registration's field list is the attack surface and nothing in the code makes
that list enumerable."

WHAT T174 SHIPPED, and why it is not enough. A scoped (non-operator) registration is refused if it
carries `resolvers` or `mutations`. That is a DENYLIST, and it was written by enumerating what had
already been found to be dangerous:
  - the fence first checked the program name only — a grantee could name its READING `User` and capture
    the operator's living Schema and root GraphQL field (found by the lane's own H6 pass);
  - `mutations` template names are a global namespace, and a squat there EVICTS the operator's later
    registration entirely — its Query field disappears with its Mutation field (found by an escape lens);
  - `resolvers[].code` is executed ESM imported through a `data:` URL with no sandbox, so a scoped
    grantee ran arbitrary code in the gateway process, holding its filesystem and network — the operator
    seed and the store file included (found by an escape lens, proven with a live probe).

Each was closed. But three rounds of "find a reachable field, fence it" is the method that produced the
holes, not a defence against the next one. The ticket's own R2 stated the governing principle — a schema
is DATA, a bundle is CODE — and BOTH the lane and the reviewer applied it to §23 renderer bundles while
missing that a registration carries code in a second place. The principle was right; the enumeration was
short. A denylist inherits that shortness forever: every field added to `RegistrationInput` after today
is admitted to scoped callers by default, and is safe only if someone remembers to ask.

THE WORK: invert it. A scoped registration accepts an ALLOWLIST of fields and refuses everything else,
including fields that do not exist yet. Concretely, `parseRegistrationInput` yields a
`RegistrationInput`; a scoped caller's input should be checked against an explicit set of permitted
keys, and any key outside it refused as a shape defect naming the field. The next field added to the
type is then refused from scoped callers until someone deliberately admits it — which is the moment to
ask what it can reach.

WHY IT IS ITS OWN TICKET rather than a rider: the allowlist changes the DEFAULT for a surface an
authority verb depends on, and it wants its own rails and its own thought about what belongs on the
list. T174 was already carrying an RCE fix; stacking a default-inversion on top would have made one PR
answer two questions.

RAILS:
1. A scoped registration carrying a field outside the allowlist is refused as a SHAPE defect naming the
   field — and the ORDERING holds: an unauthorized caller still draws the authority refusal first,
   byte-identical, so the allowlist cannot be probed by an outsider.
2. THE RAIL THAT MAKES THIS WORTH BUILDING: add a field to `RegistrationInput` in the test itself (or
   assert over the type's keys) and prove a scoped caller is refused it WITHOUT anyone editing the
   allowlist. That is the guarantee — safe by construction rather than by memory.
3. An operator registration is unchanged and carries everything, two-sided against every scoped refusal.
4. Each currently-permitted field is individually admitted, so the allowlist cannot silently narrow and
   break a working grantee.

TIER: repair when built — it removes authority from scoped callers and adds none. But it touches the
gate an authority verb rests on, so it wants the same review shape T174 got: an escape lens whose brief
is to find a field the allowlist admits that it should not.
title: A scoped registration should carry an allowlist of fields, not a denylist — the next field is admitted by default
